segs.text: Did humans sing before they could speak? Scientists still disagree. Here are the two sides, and what would narrow it down.

In eighteen seventy-one, Charles Darwin guessed yes: musical sounds first, words later. Archaeologist Steven Mithen argues for a humming, singing early language. Psychologist Steven Pinker disagrees. He called music auditory cheesecake: a pleasant by-product of faculties built for other things.

The evidence is thin. A Neanderthal hyoid bone suggests they could make speech sounds, but not whether they sang. The oldest widely accepted instruments, flutes from Germany, are about thirty-five to forty thousand years old. A Slovenian bone, maybe older, may be a flute, or may be chewed by hyenas.

New work points in several directions. In twenty twenty-four, songs across fifty-five languages were found to be slower and higher than speech. In twenty twenty-five, wild chimpanzees were found drumming in steady rhythm. In March twenty twenty-six, an essay argued musicality is rooted in biology. None of it dates the first song.

What would narrow it down? Undisputed instruments older than fifty thousand years, evidence of ancient voices and hearing, and tests across species. None alone would prove it. Until then, did we sing before we spoke? Not established. The full episode is on Heartbeat T V, at heartbeatobservatory dot com.
